builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: PhysICL: In-Context Learning of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes from Procedural Priors
summary: The method replaces per-study surrogate retraining on unstructured-mesh simulations with a single checkpoint that infers new field-prediction tasks in context from labeled simulations, but adopting it requires pretraining on procedurally generated tasks (or fine-tuning an existing checkpoint if one is released), which is a training investment outside a no-training budget. Costs are modest at inference (about 4.3 GiB at K=64 on million-node meshes, within a 24 GB GPU), but pretraining is the dominant expense and no public checkpoint or PLAID-scale pretrained weights are guaranteed. It can fail where the target physics is far from the procedural prior (accuracy lagged reduced-order models on low-rank fields) and it needed prior-matched fine-tuning to reach acceptable stress error on 2D_MSHE.
rationale: The approach is promising for simulation-heavy engineering workflows but depends on a pretrained checkpoint and prior-matched fine-tuning that the reader, with no foundation-model training budget, cannot yet obtain or validate.
technique: In-context learning for mesh field prediction

claims.statement: The method replaces per-study surrogate retraining on unstructured-mesh simulations with a single checkpoint that infers new field-prediction tasks in context from labeled simulations, but adopting it requires pretraining on procedurally generated tasks (or fine-tuning an existing checkpoint if one is released), which is a training investment outside a no-training budget. Costs are modest at inference (about 4.3 GiB at K=64 on million-node meshes, within a 24 GB GPU), but pretraining is the dominant expense and no public checkpoint or PLAID-scale pretrained weights are guaranteed. It can fail where the target physics is far from the procedural prior (accuracy lagged reduced-order models on low-rank fields) and it needed prior-matched fine-tuning to reach acceptable stress error on 2D_MSHE.

On 2D_MSHE, fine-tuning on procedural tasks matching its geometry and loads, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7; from K=32 context examples, field error is below that of the nearest context simulation on all five PLAID datasets, and peak GPU memory stays at 4.27 GiB on 1.1M-node meshes.
